newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Jobs data fails to unnerve NZ bill market.
newsitem.headline: Jobs data fails to unnerve NZ bill market.

* Bills hold steady despite easiness of MCI
* Jobs data firmer than market forecasts
* Bond yields fall on view of slowing economy
By Simon Louisson
New Zealand's money market waved a red rag to the Reserve Bank on Tuesday despite jobs data more in line with the bank's forecasts than the private sectors' predictions.
Ninety day bank bills ended pretty much where they began the session but did a lot of travelling in a wide range in between.
The Monetary Conditions Index closed 81 points easier than the RB's desired level despite the bank saying it had not changed its views.

June data showed unemployment rose to 6.7 percent against market forecasts of 6.9 percent while the closely-watched hours worked rose 2.5 percent in the quarter against RB forecasts of 1.9 percent and market forecasts of 1.0-1.5 percent.
The market preferred to place its own interpretation on both the jobs data and the bank's comment.
"A finer look at the employment data suggests a still weak labour market (as all growth was part-timers)," said market commentator MMS.
While the RB said it had not changed its view from June a close inspection of those words left room for interpretation.
The bank said its June statement that it could become more tolerant of its 50 point "comfort zone" on the MCI as more data came to hand and as the previous forecast receded into history.
Bancorp economist Stuart Marshall said the unemployment numbers had done nothing to change the underlying assumptions about the economy.
Yet the market had placed undue emphasis on the jobs numbers as a way try and back its view that the RB had been holding conditions too tight, Marshall argued.
He said the market was playing a dangerous game as the RB makes the rules, judges the play and dishes out the penalties.
"The more the economy runs the way the RBNZ has predicted, the more confident the RBNZ will be about pulling the market up and penalising it for its errant shifts in monetary conditons."
ANZ Investment Bank domestic markets manager Jim Reardon said bonds rallied partly because the RB had not formally eased.
"It continues to bode well for the bond market. If we don't ease the economy slows, and there is less danger of inflation."
But the short end would continue to test the RBNZ.

"At the moment the bank haven't done anything to defend their previously stated target so I think the market is saying in absence of any restraining statement, they will continue to ease at their leisure."
He said the bill market had partly detatched itself from the RB's 2/1 ratio.
Bankers Trust Executive Vice President John McFarlane said he believed the RB would no longer defend 750 on the MCI.
He said the RB now had to answer the question of whether the deflationary impact of the recent increase in bill rates outweighted the inflationary effects of the fall in the currency.
The economy had weakened and the RB may have to alter its two-for-one ratio of 100 basis point interest rate move offsetting a two percentage point move in the TWI, he said.
